title: What is the String Pool (intern pool) in Java, and how does it decide whether to reuse an existing reference or create a new object?
shortTitle: What is the String Pool and how does it decide reuse?

s1_definition.profdef: The String Pool, also called the intern pool, is a special area managed by the JVM that stores a single canonical reference for distinct string values. When the compiler encounters a string literal, that literal is automatically interned, so all identical literals in the program share one pooled String object. A string created with `new String(...)` is always a distinct object on the heap and is not pooled unless you explicitly call `intern()`, which returns the pooled reference for that value, adding it to the pool if absent. The decision to reuse versus create is therefore based on whether the string is a compile-time literal or interned, in which case the pool is consulted, versus runtime-constructed with `new`, in which case a fresh object is created.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the String Pool is like a central directory of official account-label cards kept at head office. The first time the label SAV2001 is needed as a literal, head office files one official card and gives everyone a pointer to that same card. Everyone who uses the literal SAV2001 points to the same single card, saving paper. But if a clerk writes a brand-new card by hand with new String, that is a separate card not in the directory, even if it says SAV2001. The clerk can file it into the central directory by calling intern, after which asking for SAV2001 returns the one official card.
s1_definition.oneliner: Literals are auto-interned and share one pooled object; new String always makes a fresh object, and intern() forces pooling by value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The String Pool, also called the intern pool, is a special area managed by the JVM that stores a single canonical reference for distinct string values. When the compiler encounters a string literal, that literal is automatically interned, so all identical literals in the program share one pooled String object. A string created with `new String(...)` is always a distinct object on the heap and is not pooled unless you explicitly call `intern()`, which returns the pooled reference for that value, adding it to the pool if absent. The decision to reuse versus create is therefore based on whether the string is a compile-time literal or interned, in which case the pool is consulted, versus runtime-constructed with `new`, in which case a fresh object is created.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the String Pool is like a central directory of official account-label cards kept at head office. The first time the label SAV2001 is needed as a literal, head office files one official card and gives everyone a pointer to that same card. Everyone who uses the literal SAV2001 points to the same single card, saving paper. But if a clerk writes a brand-new card by hand with new String, that is a separate card not in the directory, even if it says SAV2001. The clerk can file it into the central directory by calling intern, after which asking for SAV2001 returns the one official card.

**One line to remember:** Literals are auto-interned and share one pooled object; new String always makes a fresh object, and intern() forces pooling by value.

sections.s2_technical:
The String Pool is a cache of unique String instances keyed by their value. In modern JVMs it lives in the heap. Its purpose is to avoid storing many copies of the same string value, which is valuable because strings are extremely common.

String literals are handled specially at compile and class-load time. When the compiler sees a literal like SAV2001, it records it in the class file's constant pool, and when the class is loaded, that literal is interned into the String Pool. So every occurrence of the identical literal across your whole program resolves to the same pooled String object. This is why two identical literals compared with double-equals are the same reference.

Compile-time constant expressions are also folded and pooled. If you concatenate two literals, like the literal SAV plus the literal 2001, the compiler computes the result at compile time to the single literal SAV2001 and pools it. But if any part is a non-constant, such as a variable, the concatenation happens at runtime and produces a new, unpooled String.

The `new String("SAV2001")` form explicitly constructs a new object on the heap. It is guaranteed to be a distinct object, separate from the pooled literal, so double-equals with the literal is false. This is almost never what you want for value comparison, which is why double-equals on strings is dangerous.

The `intern()` method is how you interact with the pool at runtime. Calling intern on a string returns the canonical pooled reference for that value: if the pool already has a string with that value, it returns the existing one; otherwise it adds this string's value to the pool and returns it. A senior nuance is that interning large numbers of dynamic strings can bloat the pool and waste memory, and before Java 7 the pool lived in a fixed-size PermGen that could overflow, so deliberate interning of runtime strings should be used carefully. Another nuance is that you should never rely on pool identity for correctness; use equals for value comparison and treat the pool purely as a memory optimization.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank uses the same account-type labels like SAVINGS and CURRENT millions of times, and wants them stored once to save memory. This is exactly what literal pooling provides automatically.

Problem 2 — A developer built an account number at runtime by concatenating a variable and was surprised it was a different object from the literal. This is exactly the difference between compile-time constant folding and runtime concatenation.

Problem 3 — The team wants to deduplicate account-type strings read from a file so repeated values share one object, using intern deliberately. This is exactly the controlled use of intern.

The code has a `LabelCache` demonstrating pooling and intern, and a `StringPoolDemo` main class showing reuse versus new object decisions.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/pool/StringPoolDemo.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.pool.StringPoolDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: literals SAV2001, a folded constant, a runtime concatenation, an interned string, a new String, and repeated SAVINGS labels.

Step 1: Two SAV2001 literals are created. Both are interned at class load, so they share one pooled object, and double-equals is true.

Step 2: The expression SAV plus 2001, both literals, is folded by the compiler into the single literal SAV2001 and pooled, so it equals the first literal by double-equals.

Step 3: A runtime concatenation using a variable prefix produces a new unpooled String. Double-equals with the literal is false, but equals is true, because the value matches while the identity differs.

Step 4: Calling intern on that runtime string returns the pooled reference for SAV2001, so now double-equals with the literal is true. This shows intern consults and reuses the pool.

Step 5: A new String of SAV2001 is explicitly constructed as a distinct heap object, so double-equals with the literal is false even though the value is identical.

Step 6: Two separately constructed SAVINGS strings are normalized through intern, and both resolve to the same pooled object, demonstrating deliberate interning deduplicates repeated runtime values to save memory.

```text
INFO: two literals == : true
INFO: folded constant == literal : true
INFO: runtime concat == literal : false
INFO: runtime concat .equals : true
INFO: after intern() == literal : true
INFO: new String == literal : false
INFO: normalized labels share object : true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  "SAV2001" literal ─────────────► String Pool [ "SAV2001" @P1 ]
  "SAV2001" literal ─────────────► reuse @P1  (== true)
  "SAV"+"2001" (const fold) ─────► reuse @P1  (== true)

  prefix + "2001" (runtime) ─────► NEW @R1 (heap, NOT pooled)  (== false)
        .intern() ───────────────► returns @P1  (== true)

  new String("SAV2001") ─────────► NEW @N1 (heap, NOT pooled)  (== false)

  normalize(new "SAVINGS").intern() ─┐
  normalize(new "SAVINGS").intern() ─┴─► both → pool @P2 (== true, dedup)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Label Deduplication in Ingestion ═══

  ┌────────────┐  CSV rows ┌──────────────────┐  intern ┌──────────────┐
  │ File feed  │─────────→ │ Ingestion Service │───────→ │ String Pool  │
  │ (millions) │           │ LabelCache.norm() │         │ (one per val)│
  └────────────┘           └────────┬─────────┘         └──────────────┘
                                    │ deduped labels
                                    ▼
                           ┌──────────────────┐
                           │ In-memory records│ ← share label objects
                           └──────────────────┘
  Interning bounded labels (SAVINGS/CURRENT) cuts memory on huge feeds.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Pool Reuse Decision ═══

  Input string
    │
    ├─ is it a compile-time literal/constant? ──YES──► interned → pool reference
    │
    ├─ built at runtime (variable concat / new)? ─YES─► NEW heap object (unpooled)
    │        │
    │        └─ call .intern()? ──YES──► pool reference (reuse or add)
    │
    └─ new String("x") ──────────────────────────────► ALWAYS new heap object

  Rules:
   literals + const-folded  → auto-interned, shared
   runtime concat / new     → fresh object
   .intern()                → canonical pooled reference by VALUE
   correctness              → ALWAYS compare with equals, not ==
   caution                  → over-interning dynamic strings bloats memory
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The String Pool, also called the intern pool, is a JVM-managed cache that stores a single canonical String object per distinct value, and in modern JVMs it lives in the heap. Its purpose is to avoid keeping many copies of the same string value, which matters because strings are the most common objects in most programs.

The decision between reusing a pooled reference and creating a new object comes down to how the string was produced. String literals are special: when the compiler sees a literal, it records it in the class file's constant pool, and at class load the literal is interned, so every identical literal across the whole program resolves to the same pooled object. That is why two identical literals compared with double-equals are the same reference. Compile-time constant expressions are also folded and pooled, so concatenating two literals produces a single pooled literal. But if any part of a concatenation is a variable, the work happens at runtime and produces a new, unpooled String.

The new String form always constructs a distinct object on the heap, separate from the pooled literal, which is why double-equals with the literal is false even though the value matches. And the intern method is how I interact with the pool at runtime: it returns the canonical pooled reference for a value, adding it if absent, which lets me deliberately deduplicate repeated runtime strings.

In our banking ingestion, this is a real memory optimization. Account-type labels like SAVINGS and CURRENT appear millions of times in feeds, so I deliberately intern those bounded, repeated values so they all share one pooled object, which noticeably cuts memory on large files. The two cautions I always state are that over-interning unbounded dynamic strings can bloat memory, especially before Java 7 when the pool lived in a fixed PermGen, and that I never rely on pool identity for correctness: I always compare string values with equals and treat the pool purely as a memory optimization, never as a comparison mechanism.

---

keyPoints: Pool: special memory area in the heap where unique string literals are stored
abc literal goes to pool — same literal reuses the same object
new String(abc) creates a NEW heap object outside the pool
intern() moves a heap string into the pool or returns existing pool entry
Pool enables == to work for literals but NOT for new String()
